#RussiaWithAfrica

Food security beyond supply: Why Africa and the Global South need fairer agricultural markets

✍️ An article by Russian Ambassador to South Africa and Lesotho Roman Ambarov, published in Independent Online (IOL), The Public Eye and Lesotho Tribune newspapers. 

Key takeaways:

Russia: A reliable partner in ensuring food security

🔴 Russia remains a reliable agricultural partner for Africa, supplying over 18 million tonnes of grain in 2025 and a further 13 million tonnes in the first nine months of 2026.

🔴 Russian fertiliser exports to Africa exceeded 2.2 million tonnes in 2026, helping support agricultural production across the continent.

🔴 Africa has enormous agricultural potential. Investment in irrigation, mechanisation, infrastructure, modern technologies and local processing can help the continent reduce import dependence and become a major agricultural exporter.

🔴 Russia is ready to share its expertise and technologies in agricultural machinery, seed production, fertilisers, livestock farming, storage, processing and logistics.

🔴 Russia's approach is based on partnership, not dependency – combining Africa's agricultural resources and development priorities with Russian technological expertise and production capabilities.

Protecting the routes that feed the world

🔴With Western backing, Kiev has intensified attacks on Russian civilian vessels, grain terminals and agricultural export infrastructure in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov. August drone strikes on Novorossiysk grain terminals temporarily disrupted facilities with a combined annual capacity of 15.6 million tonnes.

🔴 Russia is adapting its export logistics. The development of alternative transport corridors, including Arctic routes, helps maintain the continuity of agricultural exports despite external pressures.

Who determines the price of food?

🔴 Russia is a major global grain supplier. It exported approximately 53 million tonnes of grain in 2024/25, including 44 million tonnes of wheat, to more than 100 countries, with grain export potential of at least 60 million tonnes.

🔴 Global agricultural prices are largely shaped by Western financial centres. CBOT, Euronext and ICE play a major role in price formation, raising questions about the fairness and representativeness of the current system.

🔴 The Global South needs a greater voice in agricultural pricing. It is in the interests of the Global South to develop more representative agricultural trading infrastructure and strengthen its participation in international price formation.

Russia proposes a BRICS Grain Exchange

The initiative aims to give major grain-producing countries a greater role in setting fair, predictable agricultural prices.

🔴 The initiative is gaining momentum. Supported by the 2024 Kazan Declaration, the proposal advanced in 2026, with the BRICS New Delhi Declaration reaffirming the need to develop the platform and refine its operational modalities.

🔴 Russia-Africa cooperation should go beyond supplies to include technology transfer, investment, local processing and strengthening agricultural sovereignty, ensuring African countries become market-shapers rather than price-takers.

🎙 Remarks by Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov at a meeting with participants in the Dialogue for the Future programme organised by the Alexander Gorchakov Public Diplomacy Fund (Moscow, November 26, 2026)

Key points:

• The old order that has prevailed for 500 years – dominated first by Europe and later by the “collective West” – is inevitably giving way to new centres of growth. This is not the result of revolutions, but a natural historical process driven by the laws of socioeconomic development.

• We have pursued a consistent policy. We have never tried to impose anything on anyone. We have always advocated, firstly, collective consideration of problems, whether at the #UN, the #OSCE or any other forum, and, secondly, honouring the agreements reached. Words must match deeds.

• We were deceived time and again in the early years following the dissolution of the Soviet Union, when Russia was assuming an independent role on the international stage and reaching agreements with the Americans and Europeans. The NATO-Russia Council was established, and an extensive framework of relations between Russia and the EU was developed. Yet all of this was brought down overnight simply because it was decided that Russia had no right to defend its legitimate interests.

• Had it not been for Ukraine, another pretext would have been found to evade commitments to equal and mutually beneficial cooperation. ☝️ All the West ever wanted was to dictate its terms.

• Since President Donald Trump took office, the US has demonstrated a degree of political maturity that has long been absent in Europe. Despite the remaining differences, the Americans are open to dialogue and, moreover, are interested in maintaining diplomatic and other contacts.

• No two countries on Earth can have interests that coincide 100% on every issue, especially when it comes to major powers such as the US and Russia. This was true both during the Cold War and in the era of détente. Dialogue, however, is essential under all circumstances. To their credit, the Americans understand this and are engaging in dialogue on Ukraine, recognising the need to eliminate the root causes of the crisis, namely the creation of threats to Russia’s security right on our borders.

• We are a people accustomed to facing all manner of trials. Our people have endured them in the past, are enduring them now and will undoubtedly continue to do so in the future. At the same time, we remain open to dialogue with everyone, but it must be a dialogue between decent people, conducted in a manner befitting decent people.
